# Big-O Time & Space Complexity in Game Loops

> [!TIP]
> **Why Big-O Matters in Games:** At 60 FPS, `_process(delta)` runs 60 times every second. Understanding **Big-O notation** tells you how your code scales when 10 cards become 10,000 bullets or tiles.

| Complexity | Name | GDScript Operation | Cost for `n = 1,000` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`O(1)`** | Constant Time | `dict[key]`, `arr[i]`, `arr.pop_back()` | **1 operation** (Instant) |
| **`O(log n)`** | Logarithmic | `sorted_arr.bsearch(val)` | **~10 operations** |
| **`O(n)`** | Linear Time | `card in arr`, `arr.find(x)`, `arr.pop_front()` | **1,000 operations** |
| **`O(n log n)`** | Log-Linear | `arr.sort()`, `arr.sort_custom(...)` | **~10,000 operations** |
| **`O(n²)`** | Quadratic | Nested `for a in arr: for b in arr:` | **1,000,000 operations** (Frame drop!) |

> [!WARNING]
> **`pop_back()` vs `pop_front()` on `Array`**: Removing the last element with `deck.pop_back()` is **`O(1)`** because no other elements move. Removing the first element with `deck.pop_front()` is **`O(n)`** because Godot must shift every remaining element left by 1 index!

codeSnippets.caption: Indexing `CardData` in a `Dictionary` turns `O(n)` searches into `O(1)` hash lookups.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `has_card_fast(lookup: Dictionary, card_id: String) -> bool` that checks if `card_id` exists in `lookup` in `O(1)` time using `.has(card_id)`.
practicePrompt.starterCode: func has_card_fast(lookup: Dictionary, card_id: String) -> bool:
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Returns true in O(1) constant time if card_id is a key in lookup.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func has_card_fast(lookup: Dictionary, card_id: String) -> bool:
	return lookup.has(card_id)

quizQuestions.prompt: Why did we use `deck.pop_back()` instead of `deck.pop_front()` to draw cards from our 54-card Kadi deck in Phase 2?
choices: `pop_back()` is `O(1)` constant time, whereas `pop_front()` is `O(n)` because every remaining element in the Array must shift left by one index
quizQuestions.explanation: In a contiguous dynamic array, removing the last item is `O(1)`, while removing index `0` requires shifting `n - 1` elements in memory (`O(n)`).

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the time complexity of looking up a key in a GDScript `Dictionary` (`dict.get(key)`)?
choices: `O(1)` average time via hash table lookup
quizQuestions.explanation: A `Dictionary` hashes the key to jump directly to its bucket in `O(1)` average time.

quizQuestions.prompt: At 60 frames per second (FPS), how many milliseconds of total CPU/GPU time do you have per frame before the game stutters?
quizQuestions.explanation: `1 second / 60 frames = 0.01667 seconds = 16.67 milliseconds` per frame.

# Value Types vs. Reference Types & Memory Management

In GDScript 2.0, variables behave in one of two ways when assigned (`var b = a`) or passed to a function:

| Category | GDScript Types | Assignment Behavior (`var b = a`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Value Types** (Copied by Value) | `int`, `float`, `bool`, `String`, `Vector2`, `Vector3`, `Rect2`, `Transform2D`, `Transform3D`, `Color`, `Basis` | `b` gets an **independent copy**. Modifying `b` never changes `a`. |
| **Reference Types** (Shared Reference) | `Array`, `Dictionary`, `Object`, `RefCounted`, `Resource`, `Node` | `b` points to the **exact same object in memory**. Mutating `b.append(...)` mutates `a`! |

## Shallow Copy (`.duplicate(false)`) vs. Deep Copy (`.duplicate(true)`)
- `hands.duplicate(false)` copies only the outer array; `hands[0]` still points to the same inner player hand array!
- `hands.duplicate(true)` recursively clones all nested arrays and dictionaries.

## How Godot Frees Memory (`RefCounted` vs. `Node`)
- **`RefCounted` & `Resource`** (`CardData`, `RuleValidator`): Automatically freed the instant the last reference variable goes out of scope (Reference Counting).
- **`Node`** (`CardScene`, `Table`): Owned by the `SceneTree`; must be freed explicitly via `queue_free()` (deferred cleanly to the end of the frame).

codeSnippets.code:
# Safe AI Lookahead State Cloning without Mutating Live GameState:
static func preview_hand_after_play(hand: Array[CardData], played: Array[CardData]) -> Array[CardData]:
    # Clone the array so erasing cards does NOT mutate GameState.hands!
    var simulated_hand: Array[CardData] = hand.duplicate()
    for c in played:
        simulated_hand.erase(c)
    return simulated_hand
codeSnippets.caption: Using `.duplicate()` prevents accidental aliasing bugs when previewing moves.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `clone_nested_hands(hands: Array) -> Array` that returns a deep copy of `hands` using `hands.duplicate(true)`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Returns a deep copy of the 2D hands array.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func clone_nested_hands(hands: Array) -> Array:
	return hands.duplicate(true)

quizQuestions.prompt: If `var a: Vector2 = Vector2(10, 20)` and you run `var b: Vector2 = a` followed by `b.x = 99`, what is `a.x`?
choices: `10` — because `Vector2` is a Value Type in GDScript and is copied by value on assignment
quizQuestions.explanation: Math structs (`Vector2`, `Vector3`, `Rect2`, `Color`, `Transform2D`, `Basis`) are value types in GDScript.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does `var copy = GameState.hands.duplicate(false)` still allow mutations to `copy[0].append(card)` to affect `GameState.hands[0]`?
choices: Because `duplicate(false)` performs a shallow copy of the outer array, so the inner sub-arrays (`hands[0]..hands[3]`) are still shared references; use `duplicate(true)` for a deep copy
quizQuestions.explanation: Passing `true` to `duplicate(true)` recursively clones nested arrays and dictionaries.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why do you never need to call `queue_free()` on a `CardData` (`extends Resource`) or `RuleValidator` (`extends RefCounted`) instance?
choices: Because `Resource` and `RefCounted` inherit automatic reference counting and free themselves as soon as zero variables reference them
Because `RefCounted` objects live forever in RAM
Because `CardData` is stored on the GPU
quizQuestions.explanation: `RefCounted` tracks reference counts automatically, whereas `Node` inherits `Object` directly and is managed by the `SceneTree` via `queue_free()`.

# Stacks (LIFO) & Queues (FIFO) in Game Architecture

## 1. Stack — Last-In, First-Out (`LIFO`)
Think of a physical **discard pile** of playing cards: the last card placed on top (`push_back`) is the first card taken off (`pop_back`). Both operations are **`O(1)`**!
- **Game Uses**: Undo/Redo history, UI screen navigation back-stacks, state-machine pushdown automata (pausing gameplay to push an Inventory state, then popping back).

## 2. Queue — First-In, First-Out (`FIFO`)
Think of a matchmaking line or buffered combat actions: the first action added is the first action executed.
- **Game Uses**: Turn order queues, sequential card-effect resolution queues, dialogue line queues, input buffering.

codeSnippets.caption: A LIFO Stack (`push_back` + `pop_back`) powers `O(1)` Undo/Redo in strategy and puzzle games.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `push_and_pop_lifo(stack: Array[int], new_val: int) -> int` that pushes `new_val` onto the back of `stack` with `stack.push_back(new_val)` and then returns `stack.pop_back()`.
practicePrompt.starterCode: func push_and_pop_lifo(stack: Array[int], new_val: int) -> int:
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Pushes new_val and pops it in LIFO order.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which data structure principle describes Kadi's `discard_pile` (where the most recently played card sits on top and is inspected first)?
quizQuestions.explanation: Appending to the top (`push_back`) and reading/removing the top card (`back()` / `pop_back()`) is a classic Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) Stack.

quizQuestions.prompt: When a player performs a brand-new move after undoing two turns, what must happen to the `redo_stack`?
choices: `redo_stack.clear()` must be called because the new move creates a new timeline branch
quizQuestions.explanation: In standard Undo/Redo architecture, recording a new action clears any previously undone future states in `redo_stack`.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which structure is best for buffering a sequence of 5 triggered card animations so they play on screen in the exact order they were triggered?
quizQuestions.explanation: A FIFO Queue processes events in chronological order (first triggered -> first animated).

# Sorting Comparators (`sort_custom`) & Binary Search (`bsearch`)

## 1. Custom Sorting with `Array.sort_custom(callable)`
By default, `Array.sort()` only knows how to compare numbers or strings. To sort custom `CardData` objects (e.g., group by Suit first, then order by Rank ascending), pass a two-argument comparator function `func(a, b) -> bool` that returns `true` when `a` should appear **strictly before** `b`:

```gdscript
hand.sort_custom(func(a: CardData, b: CardData) -> bool:
    if a.suit != b.suit:
        return int(a.suit) < int(b.suit)
    return a.rank < b.rank
)
```

> [!WARNING]
> **Strict Weak Ordering Rule**: Your comparator MUST return `false` when `a` and `b` are equal (`<` or `>`, never `<=` or `>=`), or the sorting algorithm will assert!

codeSnippets.caption: `sort_custom` orders complex objects in `O(n log n)`, and `bsearch` finds insertion indices in `O(log n)`.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `sort_scores_desc(scores: Array[int]) -> void` that sorts `scores` in descending order (highest first) using `scores.sort_custom(func(a: int, b: int) -> bool: return a > b)`.
practicePrompt.hint: Use `scores.sort_custom(func(a: int, b: int) -> bool: return a > b)`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Sorts scores in descending order using a strict comparator.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func sort_scores_desc(scores: Array[int]) -> void:
	scores.sort_custom(func(a: int, b: int) -> bool: return a > b)

quizQuestions.prompt: Why must a `sort_custom(func(a, b))` comparator use strict inequality (`a.rank < b.rank`) instead of `a.rank <= b.rank`?
choices: Because strict weak ordering requires `comp(x, x)` to be `false`; returning `true` for equal elements causes unstable sorting or assertion errors in Godot 4.3
Because `<=` is not a valid operator in GDScript
quizQuestions.explanation: Godot's comparator validation checks that an element is never reported as strictly less than itself.

quizQuestions.prompt: What prerequisite must an `Array` satisfy before calling `arr.bsearch(value)`?
choices: The array must already be sorted in ascending order
The array must contain only `Node2D` references
The array must have an odd number of elements
The array must be shuffled first
quizQuestions.explanation: Binary search (`O(log n)`) repeatedly halves the search interval and only works on sorted arrays.

quizQuestions.prompt: How many comparisons does `bsearch()` need at most to find an item in a sorted array of `1,024` elements?
quizQuestions.explanation: Each comparison cuts the remaining candidates in half (`2^10 = 1024`).

# Recursion, Trees & A* Pathfinding (`AStarGrid2D`)

## 1. Every Recursive Function Needs Two Parts
1. **Base Case**: The stopping condition that returns immediately without recursing (preventing a stack overflow).
2. **Recursive Step**: Calling the function on a smaller sub-problem (such as each child `for child in node.get_children():`).

## 2. Built-in A* Pathfinding with `[[AStarGrid2D]]`
Instead of coding priority queues from scratch, Godot 4.3 provides `AStarGrid2D` (`extends RefCounted`):
1. Set `astar.region = Rect2i(0, 0, width, height)` and `astar.cell_size = Vector2(64, 64)`.
2. Call `astar.update()`.
3. Mark walls with `astar.set_point_solid(Vector2i(x, y), true)`.
4. Call `astar.get_id_path(start_cell, goal_cell)` to get the shortest `Array[Vector2i]` path!

codeSnippets.code:
# 1. Recursive SceneTree Counter (Base Case + Recursive Step):
static func count_subtree_nodes(node: Node) -> int:
    if node == null:
        return 0
    var total: int = 1
    for child in node.get_children():
        total += count_subtree_nodes(child)
    return total

# 2. Shortest Grid Path with Godot 4.3 AStarGrid2D:
static func compute_shortest_grid_path(start: Vector2i, goal: Vector2i, walls: Array[Vector2i]) -> Array[Vector2i]:
    var astar := AStarGrid2D.new()
    astar.region = Rect2i(0, 0, 10, 10)
    astar.diagonal_mode = AStarGrid2D.DIAGONAL_MODE_NEVER
    astar.update()
    for w in walls:
        astar.set_point_solid(w, true)
    return astar.get_id_path(start, goal)
codeSnippets.caption: Recursive tree traversal and `AStarGrid2D` shortest-path solver.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a recursive function `factorial(n: int) -> int` that returns `1` when `n <= 1` (base case) and returns `n * factorial(n - 1)` otherwise.
practicePrompt.hint: Check `if n <= 1: return 1` and then `return n * factorial(n - 1)`.
practicePrompt.expectedOutput: Computes n! recursively with a safe base case.

quizQuestions.prompt: What happens if a recursive function is missing its **base case**?
choices: It calls itself infinitely until the call stack overflows (Stack Overflow crash)
Godot automatically converts it into a `Tween`
quizQuestions.explanation: Every recursive call allocates a new stack frame; without a base case to stop recursion, the call stack exhausts its limit.

quizQuestions.prompt: In `AStarGrid2D`, which method must you call after changing `region`, `cell_size`, or `diagonal_mode` before querying paths or setting solid cells?
quizQuestions.explanation: `AStarGrid2D.update()` allocates the internal grid points for the configured `region`.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does the A* (`A-Star`) algorithm find the shortest path faster than an uninformed Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
choices: It prioritizes nodes with the lowest `f(n) = g(n) + h(n)`, combining exact cost from start (`g`) with a heuristic estimate to the goal (`h`)
quizQuestions.explanation: Adding an admissible heuristic `h(n)` (like Manhattan or Euclidean distance) guides the search directly toward the goal.

debugChallenge.bugDescription: When the AI runs `simulate_ai_discard()` to preview a move, the card is permanently deleted from the real `GameState.hands[seat]` even if the AI decides not to play it! Tap the buggy line.
debugChallenge.explanation: `all_hands` is a 2D array (`Array` of `Array`s). Calling `duplicate(false)` performs a shallow copy of the outer array only, so `sim_hands[seat]` still references the live player hand array! Passing `duplicate(true)` deep-copies all nested sub-arrays.
debugChallenge.hint: Look at the boolean argument passed to `all_hands.duplicate(...)` on the nested 2D array.
